hints: Look at the cumene product and work backwards. The benzene ring has gained a $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ group, so what small chloroalkane could supply that carbon skeleton intact?
Remember that when a chloroalkane reacts with benzene in electrophilic substitution, the Cl is displaced. What small inorganic molecule must form from that Cl plus the H lost from the ring?
walkthrough:
Spot what has been added to benzene**
Picture benzene meeting D. The product cumene is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$. That is just benzene where one H has been replaced by an isopropyl group. So D must be the source of that three carbon fragment.

Choose the correct chloroalkane**
For Friedel-Crafts alkylation with a chloroalkane, the C-Cl bond generates the alkyl electrophile. To deliver $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, you need $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$, which is 2-chloropropane. The 1-chloro isomer would rearrange to the more stable secondary carbocation anyway.

Balance the leftover atoms**
Benzene loses H, D loses Cl. Put them together and you get $\text{HCl}$. That is the non-organic product E, exactly as in other Friedel-Crafts reactions using chloroalkanes.

Final answer: D is 2-chloropropane, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHClCH}_{3}$
E is hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$

hints: Think of the general family where benzene reacts with a chloroalkane with a halogen carrier catalyst to attach an alkyl group.
walkthrough:
Name the ring reaction**
You have benzene plus a chloroalkane giving an alkylbenzene. That is the classic way to attach an alkyl chain directly to the ring. At A Level this is always called Friedel-Crafts alkylation, a type of electrophilic substitution.
Final answer: (Friedel-Crafts) alkylation

hints: Recall which Lewis acid catalysts are used to polarise $\text{Cl}_{2}$ for attack on the benzene ring, as opposed to UV light for side-chain attack.
walkthrough:
Pick the ring chlorination catalyst**
Chlorine alone is not electrophilic enough to attack the stable benzene pi system. You need a halogen carrier that accepts a lone pair from $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to generate a strong $\text{Cl}^{+}$ like electrophile. Both anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ and $\text{FeCl}_{3}$ do this job perfectly.
Final answer: $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ or $\text{FeCl}_{3}$

hints: The isopropyl group already on cumene is 2,6-directing for further electrophilic substitution, so consider which ring positions are favoured and least hindered.
walkthrough:
Use the directing effect**
The alkyl side-chain in cumene, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, is electron donating and 2,4-directing. That means the next electrophile $\text{Cl}^{+}$ goes ortho or para to it, not meta. Either the 2-chloro or the 4-chloro ring substituted product counts as one of the two major isomers of formula $\text{C}_{9}\text{H}_{11}\text{Cl}$.
Final answer: 2-chloro-isopropylbenzene (2-chlorocumene, ortho isomer) OR 4-chloro-isopropylbenzene (4-chlorocumene, para isomer)

hints: Contrast ionic ring substitution with radical attack on the alkyl side-chain, and recall what provides the energy to split $\text{Cl}_{2}$ into radicals.
walkthrough:
Switch to radical conditions**
If you want Cl to go into the side-chain rather than the ring, you must avoid the polar electrophilic pathway. Bright sunlight or UV photons homolytically cleave $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to $\text{Cl} \cdot$ radicals, which then abstract benzylic H by a free radical chain. Strong heating has the same effect.
Final answer: sunlight or UV light OR high temperature, $T > 100^{\circ}\text{C}$

hints: Focus only on the $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ side-chain and think where a $\text{Cl} \cdot$ radical could replace a hydrogen, remembering the benzylic position is most reactive.
walkthrough:
Draw the two side-chain chlorides**
Keep the benzene ring untouched and chlorinate the isopropyl chain, $\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$. Replacing the single benzylic H gives $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(Cl)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$, the major product from the stable tertiary benzylic radical. Replacing one of the six primary H atoms gives $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$. Either structure is acceptable as one of the two isomers.
Final answer: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(Cl)(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}$ OR $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$

hints: For hot $\text{KMnO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$, recall what happens to any alkyl side-chain on a benzene ring regardless of its length, while a $\text{NO}_{2}$ group survives.
For $\text{H}_{2}$ with Ni under high pressure, think which functional group is easily reduced, the aromatic ring under forcing conditions or the $\text{NO}_{2}$ group, and what it becomes.
walkthrough:
Oxidise the side-chain completely**
Hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_{4}$ is a brutal oxidiser for alkylbenzenes. The whole isopropyl group in 4-nitro-cumene is chewed back to a $\text{COOH}$ group attached directly to the ring. The nitro group is already fully oxidised so it is untouched. You get $\text{O}_{2}\text{NC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COOH}$, 4-nitrobenzoic acid.

Reduce the nitro group**
$\text{H}_{2}$ with Ni is a reducing system. The $\text{NO}_{2}$ group is very easily reduced stepwise to $\text{NH}_{2}$. So you get the corresponding amine, 4-amino-isopropylbenzene. Under very high pressure even the ring can be further hydrogenated, but the key examinable change is $\text{NO}_{2}$ to $\text{NH}_{2}$.

Final answer: With hot $\text{KMnO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$: 4-nitrobenzoic acid, $\text{O}_{2}\text{NC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COOH}$
With $\text{H}_{2}$ + Ni, high pressure: reduction of $\text{NO}_{2}$ to $\text{NH}_{2}$ (4-amino-isopropylbenzene, further ring reduction possible under forcing conditions)

hints: Start by identifying the active electrophile formed from conc. $\text{HNO}_{3}$ and conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ in nitration.
Think how the delocalised pi electrons of cumene first interact with that electrophile to form a new C-N bond.
Recall what the non-aromatic cationic intermediate looks like, with the positive charge delocalised over five carbons.
Consider how the C-H bond at the site of attack breaks to restore the stable aromatic sextet and what small ion is expelled.
walkthrough:
Generate the correct electrophile**
Nitration does not use $\text{HNO}_{3}$ directly. Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ protonates $\text{HNO}_{3}$ to lose water and give the nitronium ion, $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$. Write this ion clearly at the start of your mechanism. It is linear and strongly positive on N, hungry for electrons.

Attack by the ring pi electrons**
Think of the benzene circle in cumene as a source of electrons. Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the ring, from the delocalised system, pointing to the N atom of $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$. This forms the new C-N bond and destroys aromaticity temporarily. The isopropyl group stays as a spectator.

Draw the arenium ion correctly**
After attack you have a cyclohexadienyl cation. Show a horseshoe of delocalisation covering five carbons, with a + charge, and the $\text{NO}_{2}$ group plus the original H both attached to the sixth $sp^{3}$ carbon. Do not draw a full circle. This shows the positive charge is delocalised but aromaticity is lost.

Restore aromaticity by losing $\text{H}^{+}$**
A base removes the proton from that $sp^{3}$ carbon. Draw a curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring to reform the full aromatic pi system. The H leaves as $\text{H}^{+}$. This final step releases a lot of energy because the stable aromatic sextet is regained, giving the nitro-cumene product.

Final answer: Electrophile is $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$
Curly arrow from benzene pi system to $\text{NO}_{2}^{+}$ to form C-N bond
Arenium ion intermediate with delocalised positive charge over 5 carbons (horseshoe) and $\text{NO}_{2}$ attached
Curly arrow from C-H bond back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, expelling $\text{H}^{+}$
